'''''Dracaena draco''''', the '''Canary Islands dragon tree''' or '''drago''',<ref>{{Citation |title=Forest 15 - Dragon Tree |website=National Arboretum Canberra |publisher=Australian Government |url=https://www.nationalarboretum.act.gov.au/living-collection/trees/tree-descriptions/forests-and-trees/forest-15 |access-date=2018-09-22 |archive-date=2018-09-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180923005522/https://www.nationalarboretum.act.gov.au/living-collection/trees/tree-descriptions/forests-and-trees/forest-15 }}</ref> is a [[subtropics|subtropical]] tree in the [[genus]] ''[[Dracaena (plant)|Dracaena]]'', [[native plant|native]] to the [[Macaronesia]] archipelago (the [[Canary Islands]], Cape Verde, and Madeira; possibly introduced in the Azores) and northwestern mainland [[Africa]].<ref name = "iucn"/>

It was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1762 as ''Asparagus draco''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite taxon |POWO |title=''Dracaena draco'' (L.) L. |id=534171-1 |access-date=2021-09-17}}</ref><ref name=L1>{{cite book|author=Linnaeus, C.|title=Species plantarum|edition=2|volume= 1|page= 451|date=1762|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/11628905}}</ref> In 1767 he assigned it to the new genus, ''[[Dracaena (plant)|Dracaena]]''.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=L2>{{Cite journal|last=Linnaeus|first=C.|date=1767|title=''Dracaena''|journal=Systema Naturae: Per Regna Tria Natura, Secundum Classes, Ordines, Genera, Species, Cum Characteribus, Differentiis, Synonymis, Locis (Ed. 12)|volume= 2|page= 246| url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/42947869}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Ajgal P2210782.jpg|thumb|left|''Dracaena draco'' subsp. ''ajgal'' in the village Agadir Ougjgal near [[Tiznit]], Morocco]]

''Dracaena draco'' is an evergreen long lived tree capable of exceeding {{convert|15|m|abbr=on}} in height and having a trunk of {{convert|5|m|abbr=on}} or more in circumference, starting with a smooth bark that evolves to a more rough texture as it ages.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Dracaena draco'' (L.) L. |publisher=[[University of Madeira]] |url=http://www3.uma.pt/biopolis/planta.php?id=259 |access-date=13 January 2021}}</ref> The "dragon tree" is a [[Monocot]], with a branching growth pattern currently placed in the asparagus family ([[Asparagaceae]], subfamily Nolinoidae).<ref name=Chase2009>{{cite journal |last1=Chase |first1=M.W. |last2=Reveal |first2=J.L. |last3=Fay |first3=M.F. |year=2009 |title=A subfamilial classification for the expanded asparagalean families Amaryllidaceae, Asparagaceae, and Xanthorrhoeaceae |journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |volume=161 |issue=2 |pages=132–136 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.2009.00999.x |name-list-style=amp |doi-access=free}}</ref> When young it has a single stem. At about 10–15 years of age the stem stops growing and produces a flower spike with white, lily-like perfumed flowers, followed by coral berries. Soon a crown of terminal buds appears and the plant starts branching. Each branch grows for about 10–15 years and re-branches, so that a mature plant has an umbrella-like habit. It grows slowly, requiring about 10 years to reach {{convert|1.2|m|ft|0}} in height, but at times, grows much faster.{{clarify|date=September 2022}}<ref>{{cite web |title=Dracaena Draco Farm |url=http://www.dracaenadraco.com/ |access-date=2011-11-03 }}</ref>

Despite being a monocotyledon, it has annual growth rings. There is considerable genetic variation within the Canary Island dragon trees. The form found on [[Gran Canaria]] is now treated as a separate species, ''[[Dracaena tamaranae]]'', based on differences in flower structure. The form endemic to [[La Palma]], initially branches very low with numerous, nearly vertical branches arranged fastigiately. There is a forest of such trees at Las Tricias, Garafia district, La Palma.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Dracaena draco'' |website=www.floradecanarias.com |url=http://www.floradecanarias.com/dracaena_draco.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Buracas |series=Visit La Palma |website=visitlapalma.es |url=http://www.visitlapalma.es/en/recursos_naturales/buracas}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:D.draco-3.jpg|thumb|150px|[[Inflorescence]]]]

''Dracaena draco'' is native to [[Macaronesia]] and southwest [[Morocco]], where it is commonly cultivated as an ornamental plant. On the Canary and Madeira archipelagos, wild endemic populations today are known only in [[Tenerife]] and [[Madeira Island|Madeira]] after recently going extinct in the wild in [[Gran Canaria]]. Wild populations in Morocco extend to the southwest [[Atlas Mountains]]. Its origin on the [[Azores]] is uncertain but it is thought to result from an introduction made by the Portuguese prior to 1500 with seeds from [[Madeira]] and [[Cape Verde]], as some individuals were observed to have similarities with the Cape Verdean subspecies (subsp. ''caboverdeana''); there are around 200-300 individuals on remote sites in the island of [[São Jorge Island|São Jorge]] and a few more on other islands and it is unknown if these populations can be considered native or the result of an early introduction.<ref name = "iucn" /><ref>{{cite web |title=''Dracaena draco'' subsp. ''draco'' |url=https://acores.flora-on.pt/#/1dracaena+draco |publisher=Flora-on |access-date=13 January 2021}}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Dracaena draco 1.jpg|thumb|right|Fruits]]

When the bark or leaves are cut they secrete a reddish [[resin]], one of several sources of substances known as [[dragon's blood]]. Red resins from this tree contain many mono- and dimeric flavans that contribute to the red color of the resins.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The Flavonoids|last=Porter|first=Lawrence J.|date=1988-01-01|publisher=Springer US|isbn=978-0-412-28770-1|editor-last=Harborne|editor-first=J. B.|pages=21–62|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-1-4899-2913-6_2|chapter=Flavans and proanthocyanidins}}</ref> Dragon's blood has a number of traditional medical uses, although dragon's blood obtained from ''Dracaena draco'' was not known until the 15th century,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gupta |first1=D. |last2=Bleakley |first2=B. |last3=Gupta |first3=R.K. |title=Dragon's blood: Botany, chemistry and therapeutic uses |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |date=2007 |volume=115 |issue=3 |pages=361–380 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2007.10.018 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/5786935 |access-date=2015-02-17 |pmid=18060708}}</ref> and analyses suggest that most dragon's blood used in art was obtained from species of the genus ''[[Calamus (palm)|Calamus]]'' formerly placed in ''[[Daemonorops]]''.<ref name=":0" /> The primary and secondary plant body are the site of the secretory plant tissues that form dragon's blood. These tissues include ground parenchyma cells and cortex cells.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jura-Morawiec |first1=Joanna |last2=Tulik |first2=Mirela |date=2015-05-01 |title=Morpho-anatomical basis of dragon's blood secretion in ''Dracaena draco'' stem |journal=Flora - Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants |volume=213 |pages=1–5 |doi=10.1016/j.flora.2015.03.003|bibcode=2015FMDFE.213....1J }}</ref> Dragon's blood from ''Dracaena draco'' and ''Dracaena cinnabari'' can be distinguished by differences in 10 compounds and a dominant flavonoid DrC11 missing in ''Dracaena draco''.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Baumer |first1=Ursula |last2=Dietemann |first2=Patrick |date=2010-06-01 |title=Identification and differentiation of dragon's blood in works of art using gas chromatography/mass spectrometry |journal=Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry |language=en |volume=397 |issue=3 |pages=1363–1376 |doi=10.1007/s00216-010-3620-0 |pmid=20349349 |bibcode=2010ABiCh.397.1363B |s2cid=13267387 |issn=1618-2642}}</ref>

The [[Guanches]] worshiped a specimen in Tenerife, and hollowed its trunk into a small [[sanctuary]]. [[Alexander von Humboldt]] saw it at the time of his visit. It was {{convert|70|ft}} tall and {{convert|45|ft}} in circumference, and was estimated to be 6,000 years old. It was destroyed by a storm in 1868.<ref>{{Cite NIE|wstitle=Dracæna draco|year=1905}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Dracaena draco'' is cultivated and widely available as an [[ornamental tree]] for parks, gardens, and [[xeriscape|drought tolerant]] water conserving [[Sustainable landscaping|sustainable landscape]] projects. It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Dracaena draco''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/6092/Dracaena-draco/Details|access-date=1 June 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 33 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 6 February 2018}}</ref>

In 2017, the city of [[Angra do Heroísmo]] ([[Terceira Island]]) planted a grove of 200 dragon trees.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.diarioinsular.pt/version/1.1/r16/?cmd=noticia&id=108298|title=DiarioInsular.pt|website=www.diarioinsular.pt}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.google.pt/maps/place/Bosque+de+Dragoeiros/@38.6538916,-27.2286541,18.75z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0xb467f41bb1ee871:0xe7cc91eb263a6324!8m2!3d38.6539298!4d-27.2289739|title=Bosque de Dragoeiros · Tv. do Fanal, Angra do Heroísmo, Portugal|website=Bosque de Dragoeiros · Tv. do Fanal, Angra do Heroísmo, Portugal}}</ref>

The Museum of Wine on [[Pico Island]], Azores, has one of the largest concentrations of this species in Macaronesia, some being more than 100 years old.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mata de Dragoeiros |url=http://www.museu-pico.azores.gov.pt/conteudos/18/ |publisher=Pico Museums |access-date=13 January 2021}}</ref>

==Symbolism==
''Dracaena draco'' is the natural symbol of the island of [[Tenerife]], together with the [[Tenerife blue chaffinch|blue chaffinch]].<ref>{{cite act |type=Ley |index=7/1991 |date=30 April 1991 |title=Símbolos de la naturaleza para las Islas Canarias |trans-title=Natural Symbols for the Canary Islands |url=https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1991-16276 |language=es |via=[[Boletín Oficial del Estado|BOE]] |volume=151 |pages=20946–20497}}</ref>
